# Class JevJudge

[java.lang.Object](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html "class or interface in java.lang")

org.springaicommunity.typesafe.judge.JevJudge

---

public class JevJudge extends [Object](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html "class or interface in java.lang")

A Model-as-a-judge built out of atomic questions rather than one rubric prompt.

Every criterion is answered against the same state in a single call, in parallel, so
 relevance, groundedness and plausibility can each be asked and thresholded separately
 instead of being collapsed into one number by a judge model. Composing the pass
 condition stays in Java, where it can be read and tested.

A criterion whose answer is already in the input — was a tool called, does the answer
 parse — is better declared as a `code check` than asked of Jev. Checks run
 locally before the call and land in the same verdict as the questions.

```
JevJudge judge = JevJudge.builder(typeSafeClient)
    .score("helpfulness", Score.builder()
            .instructions("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
            .level("Terrible: irrelevant or off-topic")
            .level("Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point")
            .level("Mostly helpful: minor gaps")
            .level("Excellent: fully and correctly addressed")
            .build(), 2.0)
    .noul("is_plausible",
            Noul.builder()
                .instructions("Are the values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
                .whenFalse("Contains an impossible or absurd value")
                .build(),
            0.7)
    .build();

JevVerdict verdict = judge.judge(question, answer);

```

Author:
Christian Tzolov

public class JevJudge extends [Object](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html "class or interface in java.lang")

A Model-as-a-judge built out of atomic questions rather than one rubric prompt.

Every criterion is answered against the same state in a single call, in parallel, so
 relevance, groundedness and plausibility can each be asked and thresholded separately
 instead of being collapsed into one number by a judge model. Composing the pass
 condition stays in Java, where it can be read and tested.

A criterion whose answer is already in the input — was a tool called, does the answer
 parse — is better declared as a `code check` than asked of Jev. Checks run
 locally before the call and land in the same verdict as the questions.

```
JevJudge judge = JevJudge.builder(typeSafeClient)
    .score("helpfulness", Score.builder()
            .instructions("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
            .level("Terrible: irrelevant or off-topic")
            .level("Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point")
            .level("Mostly helpful: minor gaps")
            .level("Excellent: fully and correctly addressed")
            .build(), 2.0)
    .noul("is_plausible",
            Noul.builder()
                .instructions("Are the values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
                .whenFalse("Contains an impossible or absurd value")
                .build(),
            0.7)
    .build();

JevVerdict verdict = judge.judge(question, answer);

```

public class JevJudge extends [Object](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html "class or interface in java.lang")

A Model-as-a-judge built out of atomic questions rather than one rubric prompt.

Every criterion is answered against the same state in a single call, in parallel, so
 relevance, groundedness and plausibility can each be asked and thresholded separately
 instead of being collapsed into one number by a judge model. Composing the pass
 condition stays in Java, where it can be read and tested.

A criterion whose answer is already in the input — was a tool called, does the answer
 parse — is better declared as a `code check` than asked of Jev. Checks run
 locally before the call and land in the same verdict as the questions.

```
JevJudge judge = JevJudge.builder(typeSafeClient)
    .score("helpfulness", Score.builder()
            .instructions("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
            .level("Terrible: irrelevant or off-topic")
            .level("Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point")
            .level("Mostly helpful: minor gaps")
            .level("Excellent: fully and correctly addressed")
            .build(), 2.0)
    .noul("is_plausible",
            Noul.builder()
                .instructions("Are the values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
                .whenFalse("Contains an impossible or absurd value")
                .build(),
            0.7)
    .build();

JevVerdict verdict = judge.judge(question, answer);

```

## Summary

### Jackson 3.x vs 2.x Public Methods

| Method | Jackson 2.x (2.22.3) | Jackson 3.x (3.2.3) |
|--------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `allowIfBaseType(Class)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `allowIfBaseType(Pattern)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `allowIfBaseType(String)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `allowIfBaseType(TypeMatcher)` | ✅ (since 2.11) | ✅ |
| `denyForExactBaseType(Class)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `allowIfSubType(Class)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `allowIfSubType(Pattern)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `allowIfSubType(String)` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `allowIfSubType(TypeMatcher)` | ✅ (since 2.11) | ✅ |
| `allowIfSubTypeIsArray()` | ✅ (since 2.11) | ✅ |
| `build()` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `allowSubTypesWithExplicitDeserializer()` | ❌ **Does not exist** | ✅ **Jackson 3 only** |

### Method Missing in Jackson 2.x

**`allowSubTypesWithExplicitDeserializer()`** does not exist in Jackson 2.x. It was added in Jackson 3.x.

This method allows all subtypes for which a `ValueDeserializer` is explicitly provided by either `jackson-databind` itself or registered `JacksonModule`s. The determination is made by calling `DeserializerFactory.hasExplicitDeserializerFor()`.

### Changes to `allowIfSubTypeIsArray()` Behavior

The behavior of `allowIfSubTypeIsArray()` changed in both version lines:

| Version | Change |
|-----------|--------|
| **2.18.8** / **3.1.4** | **Security fix**: Previously, calling this method added a matcher that approved **every array regardless of element type**, allowing an attacker to bypass an explicit sub-class allow-list by wrapping a denied class as an array (e.g., `Evil[]`). Now, the validator unwraps arrays recursively and validates the **innermost element type** against the configured `subTypeClassMatchers` and `subTypeNameMatchers`. |

#### Before the fix (2.18.8/3.1.4):
- Arrays were blindly accepted once this method was called
- Attack vector: `Evil.class` blocked, but `Evil[].class` accepted → component instantiated via bean deserialization without further validation

#### After the fix:
- Arrays are unwrapped recursively
- Primitive, abstract, and interface element types are accepted without explicit allow-list entry (they can't carry gadget chains)
- Concrete class element types must be explicitly allowed via `allowIfSubType(Class)`, `allowIfSubType(Pattern)`, or `allowIfSubType(String)`
- If you relied on "allow every array", you must now also explicitly allow-list the element types

The backward-incompatible change was made for security reasons ([databind#5981](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-databind/issues/5981)).

### allowIfSubTypeIsArray
    public [BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder](BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder.html "class in tools.jackson.databind.jsontype") allowIfSubTypeIsArray()
    Method for enabling validation of Java array sub-types: when called, the
 validator unwraps any array (recursively for nested arrays) and validates
 the innermost element type against the configured sub-class matchers.
 Arrays of primitive, abstract, or interface element types are accepted
 without an explicit allow-list entry: primitives can't carry gadget chains;
 abstract / interface elements are not directly instantiable and rely on
 per-element type-id resolution which itself runs the polymorphic type
 validator on the concrete sub-type.
        NOTE: the array-element check runs as part of `validateSubType()`,
 so it only applies when name-based sub-type matchers (see [`allowIfSubType(Pattern)`](#allowIfSubType(java.util.regex.Pattern)) / [`allowIfSubType(String)`](#allowIfSubType(java.lang.String))) have
 NOT already approved the array's class name -- per [`DatabindContext.resolveAndValidateSubType(tools.jackson.databind.JavaType, java.lang.String, tools.jackson.databind.jsontype.PolymorphicTypeValidator)`](../DatabindContext.html#resolveAndValidateSubType(tools.jackson.databind.JavaType,java.lang.String,tools.jackson.databind.jsontype.PolymorphicTypeValidator)),
 a `validateSubClassName` of `ALLOWED` skips the subsequent `validateSubType` call. In practice typical name matchers do not
 match array class names (which start with `[L` / `[I` etc.),
 so this is normally not a concern.

        NOTE (behavior change in 3.1.4 for [databind#5981]): prior versions added a
 matcher that approved every array regardless of element type, which let
 an attacker bypass an explicit sub-class allow-list by wrapping a denied
 class as an array (e.g. `Evil[]`) -- the array matched, the
 component was instantiated via plain bean deserialization without any
 further validator invocation. Callers that relied on "allow every array"
 must now also allow-list the element types they intend to accept.

        NOTE: not used with other Java collection types ([`List`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/List.html "class or interface in java.util")s, [`Collection`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Collection.html "class or interface in java.util")s), mostly since use of generic types as polymorphic
 values is not (well) supported.

  *

### allowSubTypesWithExplicitDeserializer
    public [BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder](BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder.html "class in tools.jackson.databind.jsontype") allowSubTypesWithExplicitDeserializer()
    Method for appending matcher that will allow all subtypes for which a [`ValueDeserializer`](../ValueDeserializer.html "class in tools.jackson.databind"))
 is explicitly provided by either `jackson-databind` itself or one of registered [`JacksonModule`](../JacksonModule.html "class in tools.jackson.databind")s.
 Determination is implementation by calling [`DeserializerFactory.hasExplicitDeserializerFor(tools.jackson.databind.DatabindContext, java.lang.Class<?>)`](../deser/DeserializerFactory.html#hasExplicitDeserializerFor(tools.jackson.databind.DatabindContext,java.lang.Class)).
        In practice this matcher should remove the need to register any standard Jackson-supported
 JDK types, as well as most if not all 3rd party types; leaving only POJOs and those 3rd party
 types that are not supported by relevant modules. In turn this should not open security
 holes to "gadget" types since insecure types should not be supported by datatype modules.
 For highest security cases (where input is untrusted) it is still preferable to add
 more specific allow-rules, if possible.

        NOTE: Modules need to provide support for detection so if 3rd party types do not seem to
 be supported, Module in question may need to be updated to indicate existence of explicit
 deserializers.

  *

```

  Builder class for configuring and constructing immutable [`BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator`](../../../../../com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.html "class in com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.jsontype") instances. Criteria for allowing
 polymorphic subtypes is specified by adding rules in priority order, starting
 with the rules to evaluate first: when a matching rule is found, its status
 ([`PolymorphicTypeValidator.Validity.ALLOWED`](../../../../../com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/PolymorphicTypeValidator.Validity.html#ALLOWED) or [`PolymorphicTypeValidator.Validity.DENIED`](../../../../../com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/PolymorphicTypeValidator.Validity.html#DENIED)) is used and no further
 rules are checked.

```

      Method for enabling validation of Java array sub-types: when called, the
 validator unwraps any array (recursively for nested arrays) and validates
 the innermost element type against the configured sub-class matchers.
 Arrays of primitive, abstract, or interface element types are accepted
 without an explicit allow-list entry: primitives can't carry gadget chains;
 abstract / interface elements are not directly instantiable and rely on
 per-element type-id resolution which itself runs the polymorphic type
 validator on the concrete sub-type.
            NOTE: the array-element check runs as part of `validateSubType()`,
 so it only applies when name-based sub-type matchers (see [`allowIfSubType(Pattern)`](../../../../../com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder.html#allowIfSubType-java.util.regex.Pattern-) / [`allowIfSubType(String)`](../../../../../com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder.html#allowIfSubType-java.lang.String-)) have
 NOT already approved the array's class name -- per [`DatabindContext.resolveAndValidateSubType(com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JavaType, java.lang.String, com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.jsontype.PolymorphicTypeValidator)`](../../../../../com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/DatabindContext.html#resolveAndValidateSubType-com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JavaType-java.lang.String-com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.jsontype.PolymorphicTypeValidator-),
 a `validateSubClassName` of `ALLOWED` skips the subsequent `validateSubType` call. In practice typical name matchers do not
 match array class names (which start with `[L` / `[I` etc.),
 so this is normally not a concern.

            NOTE (behavior change in 2.18.8 for [databind#5981]): prior versions added a
 matcher that approved every array regardless of element type, which let
 an attacker bypass an explicit sub-class allow-list by wrapping a denied
 class as an array (e.g. `Evil[]`) -- the array matched, the
 component was instantiated via plain bean deserialization without any
 further validator invocation. Callers that relied on "allow every array"
 must now also allow-list the element types they intend to accept.

            NOTE: not used with other Java collection types ([`List`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/List.html?is-external=true "class or interface in java.util")s, [`Collection`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/Collection.html?is-external=true "class or interface in java.util")s), mostly since use of generic types as polymorphic
 values is not (well) supported.

### allowIfSubTypeIsArray
    public [BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder](BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder.html "class in tools.jackson.databind.jsontype") allowIfSubTypeIsArray()
    Method for enabling validation of Java array sub-types: when called, the
 validator unwraps any array (recursively for nested arrays) and validates
 the innermost element type against the configured sub-class matchers.
 Arrays of primitive, abstract, or interface element types are accepted
 without an explicit allow-list entry: primitives can't carry gadget chains;
 abstract / interface elements are not directly instantiable and rely on
 per-element type-id resolution which itself runs the polymorphic type
 validator on the concrete sub-type.
        NOTE: the array-element check runs as part of `validateSubType()`,
 so it only applies when name-based sub-type matchers (see [`allowIfSubType(Pattern)`](#allowIfSubType(java.util.regex.Pattern)) / [`allowIfSubType(String)`](#allowIfSubType(java.lang.String))) have
 NOT already approved the array's class name -- per [`DatabindContext.resolveAndValidateSubType(tools.jackson.databind.JavaType, java.lang.String, tools.jackson.databind.jsontype.PolymorphicTypeValidator)`](../DatabindContext.html#resolveAndValidateSubType(tools.jackson.databind.JavaType,java.lang.String,tools.jackson.databind.jsontype.PolymorphicTypeValidator)),
 a `validateSubClassName` of `ALLOWED` skips the subsequent `validateSubType` call. In practice typical name matchers do not
 match array class names (which start with `[L` / `[I` etc.),
 so this is normally not a concern.

        NOTE (behavior change in 3.1.4 for [databind#5981]): prior versions added a
 matcher that approved every array regardless of element type, which let
 an attacker bypass an explicit sub-class allow-list by wrapping a denied
 class as an array (e.g. `Evil[]`) -- the array matched, the
 component was instantiated via plain bean deserialization without any
 further validator invocation. Callers that relied on "allow every array"
 must now also allow-list the element types they intend to accept.

        NOTE: not used with other Java collection types ([`List`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/List.html "class or interface in java.util")s, [`Collection`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Collection.html "class or interface in java.util")s), mostly since use of generic types as polymorphic
 values is not (well) supported.

  *

### allowSubTypesWithExplicitDeserializer
    public [BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder](BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder.html "class in tools.jackson.databind.jsontype") allowSubTypesWithExplicitDeserializer()
    Method for appending matcher that will allow all subtypes for which a [`ValueDeserializer`](../ValueDeserializer.html "class in tools.jackson.databind"))
 is explicitly provided by either `jackson-databind` itself or one of registered [`JacksonModule`](../JacksonModule.html "class in tools.jackson.databind")s.
 Determination is implementation by calling [`DeserializerFactory.hasExplicitDeserializerFor(tools.jackson.databind.DatabindContext, java.lang.Class<?>)`](../deser/DeserializerFactory.html#hasExplicitDeserializerFor(tools.jackson.databind.DatabindContext,java.lang.Class)).
        In practice this matcher should remove the need to register any standard Jackson-supported
 JDK types, as well as most if not all 3rd party types; leaving only POJOs and those 3rd party
 types that are not supported by relevant modules. In turn this should not open security
 holes to "gadget" types since insecure types should not be supported by datatype modules.
 For highest security cases (where input is untrusted) it is still preferable to add
 more specific allow-rules, if possible.

        NOTE: Modules need to provide support for detection so if 3rd party types do not seem to
 be supported, Module in question may need to be updated to indicate existence of explicit
 deserializers.

      Method for enabling validation of Java array sub-types: when called, the
 validator unwraps any array (recursively for nested arrays) and validates
 the innermost element type against the configured sub-class matchers.
 Arrays of primitive, abstract, or interface element types are accepted
 without an explicit allow-list entry: primitives can't carry gadget chains;
 abstract / interface elements are not directly instantiable and rely on
 per-element type-id resolution which itself runs the polymorphic type
 validator on the concrete sub-type.
            NOTE: the array-element check runs as part of `validateSubType()`,
 so it only applies when name-based sub-type matchers (see [`allowIfSubType(Pattern)`](../../../../../com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder.html#allowIfSubType-java.util.regex.Pattern-) / [`allowIfSubType(String)`](../../../../../com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/BasicPolymorphicTypeValidator.Builder.html#allowIfSubType-java.lang.String-)) have

 a `validateSubClassName` of `ALLOWED` skips the subsequent `validateSubType` call. In practice typical name matchers do not
 match array class names (which start with `[L` / `[I` etc.),
 so this is normally not a concern.

            NOTE (behavior change in 2.18.8 for [databind#5981]): prior versions added a
 matcher that approved every array regardless of element type, which let
 an attacker bypass an explicit sub-class allow-list by wrapping a denied

 component was instantiated via plain bean deserialization without any
 further validator invocation. Callers that relied on "allow every array"
 must now also allow-list the element types they intend to accept.

            NOTE: not used with other Java collection types ([`List`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/List.html?is-external=true "class or interface in java.util")s, [`Collection`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/Collection.html?is-external=true "class or interface in java.util")s), mostly since use of generic types as polymorphic

- The tool-related classes available are primarily `ToolCallback`, `ToolDefinition`, `ToolCallingChatOptions`, and related execution/management classes

**In the official OpenAI Java SDK (com.openai:openai-java:4.76.0)**:
- There are `HostedToolPermission` related classes for admin operations (managing organization-level tool permissions like Code Interpreter, File Search, Web Search, etc.)

Based on the source code of `HostedTool.java` from Spring AI OpenAI version 2.1.0-M1, here is the answer:

## HostedTool Sealed Interface Permits

The sealed interface `HostedTool` permits **5 implementations**:

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `WebSearch` | Search the public web |
| `FileSearch` | Search vector stores hosted at OpenAI |
| `CodeInterpreter` | Run Python in a sandboxed container |
| `Mcp` | Call tools on a remote MCP server from inside OpenAI's request |
| `ImageGeneration` | Generate images |
| `Raw` | **The escape hatch for sending tool definitions as raw JSON** |

## JSON Tool Definition

The **`Raw`** record is the one that lets you send a tool definition as raw JSON. Its documentation states:

> *"A tool declared as the raw request JSON, for tools this class does not type yet."*

**Constructor:**
```java
record Raw(Map<String, Object> tool) implements HostedTool
```

**Usage example:**
```java
HostedTool.Raw.of(Map.of("type", "local_shell", "command", "ls"));
```

I found the answers to your questions. Here's the summary for `spring-ai-agent-utils` 0.13.0 and `typesafe-spring-ai` 0.4.0:

 ## LocalExecBackend (spring-ai-agent-utils 0.13.0)

 **Default shell on Linux:** `/bin/bash -c`

 **Override method:** Use `Builder.shellCommand(String... shellCommand)`, for example:
 ```java
 LocalExecBackend backend = LocalExecBackend.builder()
     .shellCommand("/bin/sh", "-c")  // Use dash instead of bash
     .build();
 ```
 The default is `cmd.exe /c` on Windows, `/bin/bash -c` elsewhere.

 **Environment inheritance:** **Yes, child processes inherit the JVM's environment by default** (`cleanEnvironment` defaults to `false`).

 To start with a clean environment (recommended for model-authored commands):
 ```java
 LocalExecBackend backend = LocalExecBackend.builder()
     .cleanEnvironment(true)  // Empty environment, no JVM env inheritance
     .environment(Map.of("PATH", "/usr/bin"))  // Add specific vars
     .build();
 ```

 ## JevJudge.Builder.rubric() (typesafe-spring-ai 0.4.0)

 **That method does not exist.** The API uses a different approach — you build criteria directly:

 ```java
 JevJudge judge = JevJudge.builder(typeSafeClient)
     .score("helpfulness", Score.builder()
         .instructions("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
         .level("Terrible")
         .level("Acceptable")
         .level("Excellent")
         .build(), 2.0)  // minimum passing level
     .noul("is_plausible", noulQuestion, 0.7)
     .choice("style", styleChoice, "formal", "concise")
     .check("hasToolCall", input -> input.toolCalls() != null, "No tool was called")
     .build();
 ```

 Available builder methods: `score()`, `noul()`, `choice()`, `check()`, `criterion()`, `minConfidence()`, `failFast()`, `failOnError()`, `failOnInconclusive()`, `feedbackRenderer()`.

# Class JevJudge

[java.lang.Object](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html "class or interface in java.lang")

public class JevJudge extends [Object](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html "class or interface in java.lang")

A Model-as-a-judge built out of atomic questions rather than one rubric prompt.

Every criterion is answered against the same state in a single call, in parallel, so
 relevance, groundedness and plausibility can each be asked and thresholded separately
 instead of being collapsed into one number by a judge model. Composing the pass
 condition stays in Java, where it can be read and tested.

A criterion whose answer is already in the input — was a tool called, does the answer
 parse — is better declared as a `code check` than asked of Jev. Checks run
 locally before the call and land in the same verdict as the questions.

```
JevJudge judge = JevJudge.builder(typeSafeClient)
    .score("helpfulness", Score.builder()
            .instructions("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
            .level("Terrible: irrelevant or off-topic")
            .level("Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point")
            .level("Mostly helpful: minor gaps")
            .level("Excellent: fully and correctly addressed")
            .build(), 2.0)
    .noul("is_plausible",
            Noul.builder()
                .instructions("Are the values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
                .whenFalse("Contains an impossible or absurd value")
                .build(),
            0.7)
    .build();

JevVerdict verdict = judge.judge(question, answer);

```

Author:
Christian Tzolov

Based on my analysis of the Javadoc for both libraries, here are your answers:

---

## spring-ai-agent-utils 0.13.0: LocalExecBackend

**Default Shell on Linux:**
`/bin/bash -c`

**How to Override:**
Use `LocalExecBackend.Builder.shellCommand(String... shellCommand)`:
```java
LocalExecBackend backend = new LocalExecBackend.Builder()
    .shellCommand("/bin/zsh", "-c")  // Use Zsh instead of Bash
    .build();
```

**Environment Inheritance:**
Yes, child processes **do inherit the JVM's environment by default** (`cleanEnvironment` defaults to `false`). 

To start with an empty environment instead (recommended for model-authored commands):
```java
LocalExecBackend backend = new LocalExecBackend.Builder()
    .cleanEnvironment(true)  // Start from empty environment - JVM secrets not inherited
    .build();
```

---

## typesafe-spring-ai 0.4.0: JevJudge.Builder

**`rubric()` does not exist** in `JevJudge.Builder`. 

`JevJudge` uses an atomic criterion approach where you compose judgment criteria separately (scores, choices, nouls, code checks) rather than using a single rubric prompt:

```java
JevJudge judge = JevJudge.builder(typeSafeClient)
    .score("helpfulness", Score.builder()
        .instructions("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
        .level("Terrible: irrelevant")
        .level("Mostly helpful: minor gaps")
        .level("Excellent: fully addressed")
        .build(), 2.0)  // requires level 2 (0-indexed)
    .noul("is_plausible", Noul.builder()
        .instructions("Are the values physically plausible?")
        .whenFalse("Contains an impossible value")
        .build(), 0.7)  // probability threshold
    .check("parsed", input -> input.answer().contains("valid"), "Answer did not parse")
    .build();
```

If you're looking for a traditional single-rubric prompt judge, that class/method doesn't exist in this version of `typesafe-spring-ai`.

# Class JevJudge

public class JevJudge extends [Object](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html "class or interface in java.lang")

A Model-as-a-judge built out of atomic questions rather than one rubric prompt.

Every criterion is answered against the same state in a single call, in parallel, so
 relevance, groundedness and plausibility can each be asked and thresholded separately
 instead of being collapsed into one number by a judge model. Composing the pass
 condition stays in Java, where it can be read and tested.

A criterion whose answer is already in the input — was a tool called, does the answer
 parse — is better declared as a `code check` than asked of Jev. Checks run
 locally before the call and land in the same verdict as the questions.

```
JevJudge judge = JevJudge.builder(typeSafeClient)
    .score("helpfulness", Score.builder()
            .instructions("How well does `assistant_answer` address `user_question`?")
            .level("Terrible: irrelevant or off-topic")
            .level("Mostly unhelpful: misses the main point")
            .level("Mostly helpful: minor gaps")
            .level("Excellent: fully and correctly addressed")
            .build(), 2.0)
    .noul("is_plausible",
            Noul.builder()
                .instructions("Are the values in `assistant_answer` physically plausible?")
                .whenFalse("Contains an impossible or absurd value")
                .build(),
            0.7)
    .build();

JevVerdict verdict = judge.judge(question, answer);

```
